title: 09. Storage, CDN & Data Engineering: Hadoop Distributed File System (HDFS)
summary: HDFS is a distributed, fault-tolerant file system for storing very large files (terabytes to petabytes) across a cluster of commodity servers, using a master NameNode to track metadata, slave DataNodes to store file blocks…
objectives: Why is the HDFS block size 128 MB instead of 4 KB like ext4?
How does HDFS achieve fault tolerance, and what failure modes does it handle?
What is rack-awareness and why does replica placement matter?
What is the role of the NameNode, and why is it a single point of failure?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** HDFS is a distributed, fault-tolerant file system for storing very large files (terabytes to petabytes) across a cluster of commodity servers, using a master NameNode to track metadata, slave DataNodes to store file blocks (typically 128 MB each) replicated three times across racks, and a write-once-read-many model optimized for high-throughput batch analytics rather than low-latency random access.

HDFS was born in 2006 out of Google's GFS paper (2003), implemented by Doug Cutting and Mike Cafarella as the storage substrate for the Nutch search engine, then open-sourced and adopted by Yahoo as the foundation of its Hadoop cluster. The design motivation was specific: Yahoo needed to index the entire web — tens of petabytes of crawled HTML, link graphs, and inverted indices — on commodity hardware (Dell servers with 4–16 disks each) without spending Sun/EMC enterprise storage prices. The result was a file system that traded low-latency random access for sequential throughput, single-writer semantics for simplicity, and commodity hardware reliability for cluster-wide fault tolerance through replication. By 2014 Facebook was running the world's largest Hadoop cluster (over 100 PB across 60,000 nodes) for social graph analytics, and Yahoo's HDFS held exabytes of crawl data — both demonstrating that the model scaled beyond what a single SAN or NAS could deliver at the price point.

The architecture has two distinct roles. The **NameNode** is the master, running on a beefy machine with lots of RAM (64–512 GB) — it holds the entire filesystem namespace in memory: a tree of directories and files, plus a list of blocks for each file and which DataNodes hold each block. A 128 MB block produces ~150 bytes of metadata, so 100 million blocks (12.8 PB of data at 3x replication) needs ~15 GB of NameNode RAM — feasible but bounded, which is why HDFS clusters typically stop scaling at the NameNode's memory ceiling. The NameNode also receives heartbeats and block reports from DataNodes every 3 seconds, uses these to track node health and trigger re-replication when a DataNode fails, and persists its state to disk (an EditLog of operations and a FsImage snapshot) so it can recover on restart. The **DataNode** is the slave — a commodity box running on every worker node, storing blocks as flat files on the local Linux filesystem (often XFS or ext4 on JBOD disks, no RAID — HDFS replication replaces RAID). DataNodes serve block reads and writes, send block reports every 6 hours, and execute replication, deletion, and migration commands from the NameNode.

Files in HDFS are split into large blocks — 128 MB by default (was 64 MB before Hadoop 2.x), far larger than the 4 KB block of a traditional filesystem. The large block size has three reasons: (1) it reduces NameNode metadata — a 1 TB file is 8,192 blocks at 128 MB vs 268 million blocks at 4 KB, the latter would overwhelm the NameNode; (2) it enables sequential I/O — a MapReduce job reading a 128 MB block reads contiguous disk sectors at full bandwidth (~100 MB/s on HDD, ~500 MB/s on SSD); (3) it reduces seek time per byte — the ~10 ms seek to find a block is amortized across 128 MB, less than 0.01% of read time. The trade-off is poor for small files — a 1 KB file still consumes a 128 MB block on disk and a full metadata entry on the NameNode, which is why HDFS is described as "for large files only" and why small-file workloads (web logs split into 1-minute files) are typically concatenated into large SequenceFiles before loading.

Replication is the core fault-tolerance mechanism. By default, each block is replicated 3 times, placed using a **rack-aware** policy: replica 1 on the local node (the writer), replica 2 on a different node in the same rack (cheap cross-rack write, survives single-node failure), replica 3 on a node in a different rack (survives rack failure, e.g., a top-of-rack switch dies). Subsequent reads can pull from any replica, and the client picks the closest one (same node > same rack > different rack) for lowest latency. If a DataNode fails (heartbeat missed for 10 minutes, or network partition), the NameNode marks its blocks as under-replicated and instructs other DataNodes to copy them to new locations until the replication factor is restored — typically within minutes for a single node failure. The cluster tolerates simultaneous failure of one rack or N-3 nodes (where N is the replication factor) without data loss.

The **write-once-read-many (WORM)** model is the second key constraint. Once a file is written and closed, it cannot be modified — only appended to (Hadoop 2.x added append support, but it's used sparingly). This simplifies consistency: there are no distributed locks, no multi-writer coordination, no MVCC. The write pipeline is: client contacts NameNode, gets a list of DataNodes for the block, writes data to the first DataNode which forwards to the second which forwards to the third (a pipeline of 3 nodes), each acks back, and the client proceeds to the next block. If a DataNode fails mid-pipeline, the client recovers by recovering the partial block from the surviving replicas and continuing with a new pipeline. The trade-off is that HDFS is unsuitable for workloads requiring updates — operational databases, transactional systems, mutable shared state. It is excellent for: append-only logs (web access logs, sensor data, clickstream), bulk-loaded datasets (TPC-DS benchmarks, data warehouse fact tables), and intermediate computation output (MapReduce/Spark shuffle). This is why HDFS became the substrate for Hive, HBase, Spark, and the broader Hadoop analytics ecosystem.

Real-world examples: Yahoo's HDFS cluster indexed the web for search; Facebook's cluster stored the social graph and ran Hive queries for analytics (DAU counts, growth metrics, ad performance); Netflix used HDFS on EMR for recommendation model training on viewing logs (before migrating to S3 + Spark in the cloud era). The decline of on-prem HDFS began around 2018 as organizations migrated to cloud object storage (S3, ADLS, GCS) — which provides similar large-file, high-throughput, multi-tenant semantics without the operational overhead of managing a NameNode and DataNodes — but HDFS remains the storage layer for many on-prem Hadoop clusters and is the conceptual model that cloud object storage implements.

rack B] DN3 -->|6. ack| DN2 DN2 -->|7. ack| DN1 DN1 -->|8. ack| C C -->|9. block complete| NN NN -.->|heartbeat 3s| DN1 NN -.->|heartbeat 3s| DN2 NN -.->|heartbeat 3s| DN3 DN1 -.->|block report 6h| NN DN2 -.->|block report 6h| NN DN3 -.->|block report 6h| NN C2[Client read] -->|request block| NN NN -->|closest replica| C2 C2 -->|read from| DN1 ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` +-------------------+ +-------------------+ +-------------------+ | NameNode | | NameNode | | Standby NameNode | | (Master, RAM) | | EditLog -> disk | | (HA failover) | | | | | | | | namespace tree | | FsImage snapshot | | mirrors active | | file -> blocks | | | | | | block -> DNs | | | | | +---------+---------+ +-------------------+ +-------------------+ | | heartbeat 3s, block report 6h | +------+--------+----------+----------+ | | | | v v v v +--------+ +--------+ +--------+ +--------+ |DN rackA| |DN rackA| |DN rackB| |DN rackB| |blk_001|<--->|blk_001| |blk_001| |blk_002| |blk_002| |blk_003| |blk_002| |blk_003| +--------+ +--------+ +--------+ +--------+ ^ ^ ^ ^ | 3x replication placement: | | replica 1: writer node (rack A) | | replica 2: same rack A (cheap) | | replica 3: different rack B | | (survives rack failure) | +------------------------------------+ Write pipeline (block 1, file foo.txt, 3x replication): Client -> NameNode: create("foo.txt") NameNode -> Client: pipeline = [DN1, DN2, DN3] Client -> DN1: write block 1 (128 MB) DN1 -> DN2: stream replica (async) DN2 -> DN3: stream replica (async) DN1 -> Client: ack (after DN2 acks after DN3 acks) Client -> NameNode: block 1 complete Read pipeline: Client -> NameNode: open("foo.txt") NameNode -> Client: blocks [blk1@(DN1,DN2,DN3), blk2@(...), ...] Client -> DN1: read blk1 (closest replica) Client -> DN2: read blk2 (next closest) ``` ### Walkthrough 1. Client (Spark, MapReduce, Hive) wants to write a new file: contacts the NameNode with a `create` request, the NameNode records the file in the namespace and returns the location of the next block ID plus the pipeline of three DataNodes chosen for replica placement. 2. Client writes the first 128 MB block to DataNode 1, which simultaneously streams the bytes to DataNode 2 (same rack), which streams to DataNode 3 (different rack); each DataNode persists to local disk and acks back up the pipeline. 3. Client continues with subsequent blocks; on file close, the NameNode commits the file and persists the operation to its EditLog. 4. Each DataNode sends a heartbeat every 3 seconds (liveness) and a full block report every 6 hours (inventory); if a DataNode's heartbeat is missed for 10 minutes, the NameNode marks its blocks under-replicated and triggers re-replication to other nodes. 5. On read, the client asks the NameNode for the block list, picks the closest replica for each block (topology-aware), and reads sequentially at full disk bandwidth. 6. The NameNode persists its state (EditLog + FsImage) and supports a Standby NameNode for high availability (Hadoop 2.x), which hot-failovers if the active NameNode dies.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- HDFS Mini Mock
- Rack-aware placement: local, same-rack, different-rack.
- Replica 1: local, 2: same rack, 3+: different rack
- Fill remaining slots if needed
- No writer preference: pick across racks
- Split into 128 MB chunks
- Write pipeline: client -> DN1 -> DN2 -> DN3
- Re-replicate: copy from a live replica to a new node

**Defines:** `Block`, `DataNode`, `NameNode`

```python
"""
HDFS Mini Mock

Demonstrates: NameNode (metadata + block placement), DataNode (block storage),
rack-aware replica placement, write pipeline, read pipeline, failure re-replication.
"""
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Dict, List, Optional, Set
import hashlib

@dataclass
class Block:
    block_id: str
    size: int
    replicas: Set[str] = field(default_factory=set)  # DataNode IDs

@dataclass
class DataNode:
    node_id: str
    rack: str
    blocks: Dict[str, bytes] = field(default_factory=dict)
    alive: bool = True

    def write(self, block_id: str, data: bytes) -> None:
        self.blocks[block_id] = data

    def read(self, block_id: str) -> bytes:
        return self.blocks.get(block_id, b"")

class NameNode:
    def __init__(self, block_size: int = 128 * 1024 * 1024, replication: int = 3):
        self.block_size = block_size
        self.replication = replication
        self.namespace: Dict[str, List[str]] = {}   # file -> block IDs
        self.blocks: Dict[str, Block] = {}           # block_id -> Block
        self.datanodes: Dict[str, DataNode] = {}
        self.next_block_id = 0

    def register_datanode(self, dn: DataNode) -> None:
        self.datanodes[dn.node_id] = dn

    def _pick_replicas(self, writer_node: Optional[str]) -> List[str]:
        """Rack-aware placement: local, same-rack, different-rack."""
        if writer_node and writer_node in self.datanodes:
            local = writer_node
            local_rack = self.datanodes[local].rack
            same_rack = [d for d in self.datanodes
                         if d != local and self.datanodes[d].rack == local_rack
                         and self.datanodes[d].alive]
            other_rack = [d for d in self.datanodes
                          if self.datanodes[d].rack != local_rack
                          and self.datanodes[d].alive]
            # Replica 1: local, 2: same rack, 3+: different rack
            picked = [local]
            if same_rack:
                picked.append(same_rack[0])
            if other_rack:
                picked.append(other_rack[0])
            # Fill remaining slots if needed
            while len(picked) < self.replication:
                for d in self.datanodes:
                    if d not in picked and self.datanodes[d].alive:
                        picked.append(d)
                        if len(picked) >= self.replication:
                            break
            return picked[:self.replication]
        # No writer preference: pick across racks
        alive = [d for d in self.datanodes if self.datanodes[d].alive]
        return alive[:self.replication]

    def create(self, path: str, data: bytes, writer_node: Optional[str] = None) -> None:
        block_ids = []
        # Split into 128 MB chunks
        for i in range(0, max(len(data), 1), self.block_size):
            chunk = data[i:i + self.block_size]
            block_id = f"blk_{self.next_block_id:07d}"
            self.next_block_id += 1
            pipeline = self._pick_replicas(writer_node)
            if len(pipeline) < self.replication:
                raise RuntimeError(f"Insufficient DataNodes: {len(pipeline)} < {self.replication}")
            # Write pipeline: client -> DN1 -> DN2 -> DN3
            for dn_id in pipeline:
                self.datanodes[dn_id].write(block_id, chunk)
            block = Block(block_id, len(chunk), set(pipeline))
            self.blocks[block_id] = block
            block_ids.append(block_id)
        self.namespace[path] = block_ids
        print(f"Created {path}: {len(block_ids)} blocks, "
              f"replicas on {set().union(*[self.blocks[b].replicas for b in block_ids])}")

    def read(self, path: str) -> bytes:
        if path not in self.namespace:
            raise FileNotFoundError(path)
        data = b""
        for block_id in self.namespace[path]:
            block = self.blocks[block_id]
            for dn_id in block.replicas:
                dn = self.datanodes[dn_id]
                if dn.alive:
                    data += dn.read(block_id)
                    break
            else:
                raise RuntimeError(f"Block {block_id} has no live replica")
        return data

    def datanode_failed(self, node_id: str) -> None:
        self.datanodes[node_id].alive = False
        print(f"\n!! DataNode {node_id} FAILED")
        # Find under-replicated blocks
        for block in self.blocks.values():
            if node_id in block.replicas:
                live = [d for d in block.replicas if self.datanodes[d].alive]
                if len(live) < self.replication:
                    # Re-replicate: copy from a live replica to a new node
                    source = live[0]
                    candidates = [d for d in self.datanodes
                                  if d not in block.replicas and self.datanodes[d].alive]
                    if candidates:
                        dest = candidates[0]
                        self.datanodes[dest].write(block.block_id,
                                                   self.datanodes[source].read(block.block_id))
                        block.replicas.add(dest)
                        block.replicas.discard(node_id)
                        print(f"   Re-replicated {block.block_id} from {source} to {dest}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    nn = NameNode(block_size=128, replication=3)  # tiny block_size for demo
    # 6 datanodes, 2 racks
    for i in range(6):
        rack = "A" if i < 3 else "B"
        nn.register_datanode(DataNode(f"dn{i}", rack))

    content = b"x" * 500  # 5 blocks of 128 bytes
    nn.create("/logs/access.log", content, writer_node="dn0")
    nn.create("/data/users.csv", b"user,alice\nuser,bob\n", writer_node="dn1")

    print("\nRead /logs/access.log:")
    print(f"  bytes: {len(nn.read('/logs/access.log'))} (expected 500)")

    # Simulate DataNode failure
    nn.datanode_failed("dn0")
    nn.datanode_failed("dn1")

    print("\nRead /logs/access.log after failures:")
    print(f"  bytes: {len(nn.read('/logs/access.log'))} (data still available)")
```

quiz.question: Why is the HDFS block size 128 MB instead of 4 KB like ext4?
options: Cloud object storage has replaced HDFS for new deployments since ~2018 for five reasons.
HDFS allows a file to be written once (with optional append added in Hadoop 2.x), then read many times — but never modified in place.
Enable HA** — a Standby NameNode hot-failovers in ~30 seconds, eliminating restart pain for planned and unplanned outages.
Three reasons: metadata economy, sequential throughput, and seek amortization.
quiz.explanation: Three reasons: metadata economy, sequential throughput, and seek amortization. (1) Metadata economy: the NameNode holds the entire namespace in RAM, with ~150 bytes of metadata per block. A 1 PB file at 4 KB blocks would generate 268 million blocks needing ~40 GB of NameNode RAM — feasible but extreme, and a 100 PB cluster would need 4 TB of RAM.

quiz.question: How does HDFS achieve fault tolerance, and what failure modes does it handle?
options: Defense in depth across authentication, authorization, encryption, and audit.

The NameNode is the master of HDFS, holding the entire filesystem namespace (directory tree, file-to-block mapping, block-to-DataNode mapping) in RAM for fast lookups.
HDFS handles four failure modes via replication and re-replication.
quiz.explanation: HDFS handles four failure modes via replication and re-replication. (1) DataNode failure — each DataNode sends a heartbeat to the NameNode every 3 seconds. If the NameNode doesn't receive a heartbeat within 10 minutes (default dfs.namenode.heartbeat.recheck-interval = 300s × 2 plus 10s × heartbeat interval), it marks the DataNode as dead.
